subject: Engelska
title: Vocabulary: phrasal verbs and collocations
sourceSummary: Common phrasal verbs such as find out and look forward to, collocations with do and make, the difference between say, tell, speak and talk, and simple word formation with prefixes and suffixes.

questions.prompt: Choose the best option: "I need to ___ what time the train leaves."
questions.opener: A phrasal verb means something other than the verb's basic meaning — which one means "to find information out"?
questions.explanation: "Find out" means to discover information. "Look after" means to take care of someone and doesn't fit with a departure time.

questions.prompt: Choose the correct form: "I'm really looking forward ___ the summer holidays."
questions.opener: The expression has a fixed preposition, and after it comes a noun or an -ing form.
questions.explanation: The expression is "look forward to" + a noun or -ing form: looking forward to the holidays, looking forward to seeing you. "Look forward for" is a common mistake that doesn't exist in English.

questions.prompt: Choose the best option: "We had to stop baking because we ___ eggs."
questions.opener: What happened to the eggs — they ran out.
questions.explanation: "Run out of something" means something has been used up: we ran out of eggs. "Get on with someone" means to get along with someone and is about people, not goods.

questions.opener: "Do" goes with tasks and work, "make" with creating something new.
choices: I have to make my homework before I do dinner.
I have to do my homework before I make dinner.
I have to make my homework before I make dinner.
I have to do my homework before I do dinner.
questions.explanation: In English you "do homework" (a task you carry out) but "make dinner" (something you produce). "Make homework" is a direct translation from the Swedish "göra läxor" and isn't used.

questions.prompt: Choose the correct word: "Can you ___ me what happened yesterday?"
questions.opener: One of the verbs always takes a person directly after it, without a preposition.
questions.explanation: "Tell" is followed directly by the person: tell me, tell him a story. "Say" requires "to" before the person (say something to me), and speak/talk are used about the act of conversing itself: speak English, talk to a friend.

questions.opener: The prefix im- works like the Swedish o- in front of certain adjectives.
questions.explanation: In front of words that start with p, the prefix im- is used: impossible, impolite. The prefix un- is more common otherwise (unhappy, unfair), but "unpossible" doesn't exist.

questions.prompt: Correct the four errors: "Yesterday my teacher said me to make my homework. I am looking forward for the weekend, but first I must find the answer out."
questions.opener: Four common mistakes: wrong verb for a person, wrong collocation, wrong preposition, and wrong word order in a phrasal verb.
questions.answer: Yesterday my teacher told me to do my homework. I am looking forward to the weekend, but first I must find out the answer.
steps: "said me" → "told me". "Tell" is followed directly by the person, while "say" requires "to": said to me.
"make my homework" → "do my homework". Homework and tasks always take "do" in English.
"looking forward for" → "looking forward to". The expression has the fixed preposition "to".
"find the answer out" → "find out the answer". When the object is a full noun, it usually comes after the particle; only short pronouns can be split into the middle (find it out).

questions.prompt: Which phrasal verbs, collocations and word formation rules do you need to know at this level?
questions.opener: Phrasal verbs · do/make · say/tell/speak/talk · prefixes and suffixes.
questions.answer: Phrasal verbs: find out = to discover · look forward to + noun/-ing = to anticipate · get on with someone = to get along with · run out of = to have none left · give up = to stop trying · look after = to take care of · turn up = to arrive · Do: do homework, do the dishes, do your best, do an exercise · Make: make dinner, make a mistake, make friends, make a decision · Say something (to someone) · tell someone something · speak a language · talk to/with someone about something · Prefix: un- (unhappy), im- before p (impossible), in- (incorrect), dis- (dislike), re- = again (rewrite) · Suffix: -ful = full of (helpful), -less = without (careless), -ness turns adjectives into nouns (kindness), -ly turns adjectives into adverbs (quickly).

questions.prompt: Choose the best option: "The plane is about to ___ — please fasten your seatbelt."
questions.opener: A phrasal verb means something different from the verb's basic meaning — which one means that a plane leaves the ground?
questions.explanation: "Take off" means that a plane leaves the ground. "Give up" means to stop trying and "look after" means to take care of — neither fits a plane about to depart.

questions.prompt: Choose the correct form: "I need to ___ this word in the dictionary."
questions.opener: Which phrasal verb is used when you look up the meaning of a word?
questions.explanation: "Look up" means to search for something, such as a word in a dictionary. "Look after" means to take care of and doesn't fit with a dictionary.

questions.opener: "Do your best" is a fixed collocation in English.
choices: She always makes her best on tests.
She always does her best on tests.
She always does her best of tests.
She always makes her best of tests.
questions.explanation: In English it's "do your best", not "make your best". "Make my best" is a literal translation that isn't used.

questions.prompt: Choose the correct word: "She always ___ the truth."
questions.opener: "Tell the truth" is a fixed expression, even without a person directly after the verb.
questions.explanation: "Tell the truth" is a fixed expression in English. "Say" is otherwise used for what is said (say something), but with "the truth" specifically, "tell" is the usual pairing.

questions.opener: The prefix in- works like the negative prefix in some other languages before certain adjectives.
questions.explanation: The prefix in- is used before "correct": incorrect. "Uncorrect" and "discorrect" don't exist in English.

questions.prompt: Correct the four errors: "Yesterday my friend said me she is moving to another city. I was sad, but I must make my best to stay positive. I am looking forward for visiting her this summer, and I will find the address out soon."
questions.opener: Four common mistakes: wrong verb for a person, wrong collocation, wrong preposition, and wrong word order in a phrasal verb.
questions.answer: Yesterday my friend told me she is moving to another city. I was sad, but I must do my best to stay positive. I am looking forward to visiting her this summer, and I will find out the address soon.
steps: "said me" → "told me". "Tell" is followed directly by the person, while "say" requires "to": said to me.
"make my best" → "do my best". "Do your best" is the fixed collocation in English.
"looking forward for" → "looking forward to". The expression has the fixed preposition "to".
"find the address out" → "find out the address". When the object is a full noun, it usually comes after the particle; only short pronouns can be split into the middle (find it out).

questions.explanation: The prefix re- means again: rewrite. "Unwrite" and "dewrite" don't exist in English.
